(a) Jurisdictional Transfers.—Administrative jurisdiction over the National Forest System lands in the State of Alaska described in subsection (b) and improvements situated on such lands is transferred without consideration from the Secretary of Agriculture to the Secretary of the department in which the Coast Guard is operating. 
    (b) Areas Referred To.—The areas of lands referred to in subsection (a) are the following:
        (1) Guard island light station.—The area described in the Guard Island Lighthouse reserve dated January 4, 1901, comprising approximately 8.0 acres of National Forest uplands. 
        (2) Eldred rock light station.—The area described in the December 30, 1975, listing of the Eldred Rock Light Station on the National Register of Historic Places, comprising approximately 2.4 acres. 
        (3) Mary island light station.—The area described as the remaining National Forest System uplands in the Mary Island Lighthouse Reserve dated January 4, 1901, as amended by Public Land Order 6964, dated April 5, 1993, comprising approximately 1.07 acres. 
        (4) Cape hinchinbrook light station.—The area described in the survey dated November 1, 1957, prepared for the Coast Guard for the Cape Hinchinbrook Light Station comprising approximately 57.4 acres.  
    (c) Maps.—The Commandant of the Coast Guard, in consultation with the Secretary of Agriculture, shall prepare and maintain maps of the lands transferred by subsection (a), and such maps shall be on file and available for public inspection in the Coast Guard District 17 office in Juneau, Alaska. 
    (d) Effect of Transfer.—The lands transferred to the Secretary of the department in which the Coast Guard is operating by subsection (a)—
        (1) shall be administered by the Commandant of the Coast Guard; 
        (2) shall be considered to be transferred from, and no longer part of, the National Forest System; and 
        (3) shall be considered not suitable for return to the public domain for disposition under the general public land laws.  
    (e) Transfer of Land.—
        (1) Requirement.—Subject to paragraph (2), the Administrator of General Services, upon request by the Secretary of Agriculture, shall transfer without consideration to the Secretary of Agriculture any land identified in subsection (b), together with the improvements thereon, for administration under the laws pertaining to the National Forest System if—
            (A) the Secretary of the Interior cannot identify and select an eligible entity for such land and improvements in accordance with section 308(b)(2) of the National Historic Preservation Act (16 U.S.C. 470w–7(b)(2)) not later than 3 years after the date the Secretary of the department in which the Coast Guard is operating determines that the land is excess property, as that term is defined in section 102(3) of title 40, United States Code; or 
            (B) the land reverts to the United States pursuant to section 308(c)(3) of the National Historic Preservation Act (16 U.S.C. 470w–7(c)(3)).  
        (2) Reservations for aids to navigation.—Any action taken under this subsection by the Administrator of General Services shall be subject to any rights that may be reserved by the Commandant of the Coast Guard for the operation and maintenance of Federal aids to navigation.  
    (f) Notification; Disposal of Lands by the Administrator.—The Administrator of General Services shall promptly notify the Secretary of Agriculture upon the occurrence of any of the events described in subparagraphs (A) and (B) of subsection (e)(1). If the Secretary of Agriculture does not request a transfer as provided for in subsection (e) not later than 90 days after the date of receiving such notification from the Administrator, the Administrator may dispose of the property in accordance with section 309 of the National Historic Preservation Act (16 U.S.C. 470w–8) or other applicable surplus real property disposal authority. 
    (g) Priority.—In selecting an eligible entity to which to convey under section 308(b) of the National Historic Preservation Act (16 U.S.C. 470w–7(b)) land referred to in subsection (b), the Secretary of the Interior shall give priority to an eligible entity (as defined in section 308(e) of that Act) that is the local government of the community in which the land is located.

fable.w: The tempting reading is that the "consultation" language, the maps being "available for public inspection," and the priority for a local government amount to participation. But the only consultation is between the Coast Guard Commandant and the Secretary of Agriculture, both inside the federal government, as are the notifications and transfers involving the Administrator of General Services. Public inspection of maps is disclosure, not input into a decision, and the local-government priority only makes that government a preferred recipient of a conveyance, akin to an applicant, not a consulted party.
fable.s: The Commandant of the Coast Guard, in consultation with the Secretary of Agriculture, shall prepare and maintain maps of the lands transferred by subsection (a)

qwen_block.w: The section requires that maps be 'available for public inspection,' which constitutes a form of public participation by allowing the general public to access government information. While the consultation mentioned is between federal officials (Commandant and Secretary), the public inspection requirement brings outsiders into the process. The tempting reading might focus only on the intra-agency consultation, but the public access clause satisfies the definition of participation.
qwen_block.s: The Commandant of the Coast Guard, in consultation with the Secretary of Agriculture, shall prepare and maintain maps of the lands transferred by subsection (a), and such maps shall be on file and available for public inspection in the Coast Guard District 17 office in Juneau, Alaska.

opus.w: The only consultation and notification in this section happen between federal officials (the Commandant, the Secretary of Agriculture, the Administrator of General Services and the Secretary of the Interior), so they stay inside the government. Making maps available for public inspection only shares information; it does not ask outsiders for input before a decision. The priority given to local governments treats them as possible recipients of the land, like applicants for a benefit, not as participants in the decision.
opus.s: The Commandant of the Coast Guard, in consultation with the Secretary of Agriculture, shall prepare and maintain maps of the lands transferred by subsection (a), and such maps shall be on file and available for public inspection in the Coast Guard District 17 office in Juneau, Alaska.
opus.b:
**Analysis.** A few parts of this section look like participation at first, but none of them brings an outside party into a federal decision.

- **Consultation:** The Commandant consults the Secretary of Agriculture. Both are federal officials, so this is coordination inside the government.
- **Notification:** The Administrator of General Services notifies the Secretary of Agriculture. Again, both are federal.
- **Public inspection of maps:** The maps must be available for the public to look at. This only shares information. The public is not consulted before any decision.
- **Priority for local governments:** A local government gets priority when the Secretary of the Interior picks who receives the land. Here the local government is a possible recipient of the property, much like someone applying for a benefit. It does not advise on or help make the decision.

qwen_chat.w: The section describes intra-governmental coordination between federal officials (Commandant of the Coast Guard and Secretary of Agriculture) regarding land transfers and map preparation. While it mentions that maps are 'available for public inspection,' this is a passive disclosure of information rather than an active consultation or coordination with the public before a decision is made. The definition requires that the government consult or coordinate with outsiders, which is not happening here; the public is merely given access to existing records.
qwen_chat.s: The Commandant of the Coast Guard, in consultation with the Secretary of Agriculture, shall prepare and maintain maps of the lands transferred by subsection (a), and such maps shall be on file and available for public inspection in the Coast Guard District 17 office in Juneau, Alaska.
qwen_chat.b: Tempting-but-wrong reading: One might argue that subsection (c) requires participation because it states that maps shall be "available for public inspection." However, the definition explicitly distinguishes between active participation (consultation, hearings, advisory boards) and passive access to information. Merely making documents available for inspection does not constitute consulting or coordinating with the public before a decision is made; it is a transparency measure, not a participatory process. Furthermore, the other interactions described (between the Secretary of Agriculture, Secretary of Defense, Commandant of the Coast Guard, and Administrator of General Services) are all intra-governmental.
